title: The Washerwoman's Son: Odense to Rolighed, and Thirty Journeys Out
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Odense, the Room by the River

stops.name: Odense, Hans Jensens Stræde: birth in the corner house
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the address itself is town tradition, since Andersen gave varying accounts of where he was born
stops.campa: A shoemaker's wife is delivered of a son in a single rented room in the old quarter. Hans Andersen mends shoes and reads Holberg aloud in the evenings; Anne Marie Andersdatter washes other people's linen in the river. The corner house at Hans Jensens Stræde is the address the town settles on and builds a museum around from 1908, though the biographers keep the question open, because Andersen told it differently at different times. He is baptised at home the same day, being sickly and not expected to keep.
stops.quote: My life is a lovely story, happy and full of incident.
stops.quote_source: H.C. Andersen, The True Story of My Life: A Sketch, trans. Mary Howitt, Project Gutenberg #7007, opening sentence of Chapter I
suggested_refs: The corner house at Hans Jensens Stræde 45 and Bangs Boder, Odense, museum since 1908
sources: Odense City Museums, H.C. Andersens Hus
Wullschlager, Hans Christian Andersen: The Life of a Storyteller (2000), cited at second hand

stops.name: Odense, Sankt Hans Kirke: the home baptism confirmed
stops.date_confidence: attested; note this is the publicering, the public confirmation, not the baptism, which took place at home on 2 April
stops.campa: Two weeks after the birth the family carries the child to Sankt Hans Kirke, where the home baptism is publicly confirmed before the congregation. The Danish sources are exact about the distinction that the English ones lose: the baptism happened in the room, on the day, because the boy was not expected to live. This is the parish making it official. Andersen tells the scene long afterward as comedy, quoting the officiating preacher on the noise he made, and quoting his mother, who never forgot the remark and kept it alive for him.
stops.quote: "The young one screams like a cat!"
stops.quote_source: The True Story of My Life: A Sketch, Project Gutenberg #7007; the preacher's remark at the baptism, which Andersen's mother never forgot
suggested_refs: The Odense parish register of Sankt Hans Kirke, April 1805, distinguishing the home baptism from its publicering

stops.name: Odense, Munkemøllestræde: the shoemaker dies
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the father's death; month and day not established, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: From his second year to his fourteenth the family lives at Munkemøllestræde, two rooms and a strip of garden near the river. This is a different house from the birthplace, and a different museum, opened in 1930; the two are constantly confused. Here the father builds him a puppet theatre and cuts out the figures, reads him The Arabian Nights and the comedies of Holberg, and walks him in the woods on Sundays. In 1816 the shoemaker dies. The boy is eleven. His mother takes in washing, and in 1818 she marries again.
stops.quote: "That was the path upon which I ought to have gone!" said my father, kissed me passionately, and was silent the whole evening.
stops.quote_source: The True Story of My Life: A Sketch, Project Gutenberg #7007; the father's reaction on seeing a Grammar School pupil
suggested_refs: Munkemøllestræde 3-5, Odense, the childhood home, museum since 1930

stops.name: Odense Castle, the prince's advice
stops.date_confidence: tradition only, and contested: the H.C. Andersen Centre 1819 timetable records no audience at Odense Castle at all; year given, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Prince Christian Frederik, later Christian VIII, keeps residence at Odense Castle as governor of Funen, and tradition holds that the fourteen-year-old obtains an audience there before leaving for the capital. Andersen's own memoir shapes the scene as encouragement. The version the biographers keep runs colder: the prince hears him out and advises him to learn a respectable trade. The Centre's chronology for 1819 records no such audience. He goes anyway, on money his mother has saved from washing, with thirteen rigsdaler.
stops.quote: "What wilt thou do there?" asked my mother. "I will become famous," returned I... "People have," said I, "at first an immense deal of adversity to go through, and then they will be famous."
stops.quote_source: The True Story of My Life: A Sketch, Project Gutenberg #7007; Andersen at fourteen, explaining his plan to his mother
suggested_refs: Odense Slot, seat of the governor of Funen, and the tradition of the audience with Prince Christian Frederik
sources: Andersen's autobiography, 'The Fairy Tale of My Life'
treated as embellished tradition in Wullschlager (2000), cited at second hand

stops.name: Nyborg, the crossing of the Great Belt
stops.date_confidence: attested: he left Odense 4 September 1819 per the H.C. Andersen Centre timetable; the Nyborg crossing follows the same day or the next
stops.campa: He leaves Odense on the fourth of September in the mail coach for Nyborg, where the packet crosses the Great Belt. His mother has let him go on the reasoning that the sea will turn him back, and Nyborg is the test she has set: a harbour where a boy who has never left Funen sees open water and either boards or does not. He boards. The crossing takes him out of the only country he knows. He will spend the next fifty-six years leaving and returning, thirty journeys abroad, and never once own a house.
stops.quote: "but he lets me have no peace; I have therefore given my consent, but I am sure that he will go no further than Nyborg; when he gets sight of the rough sea, he will be frightened and turn back again."
stops.quote_source: The True Story of My Life: A Sketch, Project Gutenberg #7007; Andersen's mother before the 1819 journey
suggested_refs: The Nyborg packet station on the Great Belt, crossing point for the Funen mail road to Copenhagen

stops.name: Korsør, the prayer on the Zealand shore
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the landing falls between his 4 September departure and his 6 September arrival in Copenhagen; the shore is Zealand, the port not named in the fetched autobiography
stops.campa: Landed on Zealand, alone, with the Copenhagen coach not yet loaded, he walks down to the water, steps behind a shed on the shore, and kneels on the sand. The prayer is the hinge of his own account of himself. Everything before it is Odense and poverty; everything after is the capital and the long climb. He gets up comforted and rides on. He has no letter of introduction, no trade, and no arrangement of any kind waiting at the other end of the road.
stops.quote: I stepped behind a shed, which stood on the shore, and falling upon my knees, besought of God to help and guide me aright; I felt myself comforted by so doing, and I firmly trusted in God and my own good fortune.
stops.quote_source: The True Story of My Life: A Sketch, Project Gutenberg #7007; Andersen newly landed on Zealand, September 1819
suggested_refs: The Zealand landing shore of the Great Belt crossing, September 1819

segments.name: The Capital and the Broken Voice

stops.name: Copenhagen, Kongens Nytorv: turned away at the theatre
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: He arrives in the capital on the sixth of September with thirteen rigsdaler and no position, and goes to the theatre on Kongens Nytorv to ask for work as singer, dancer, or actor. He finds the address of the dancer Madame Schall, lets himself in, takes off his boots to be lighter, and improvises a grotesque ballet with his hat for a tambourine. He is thrown out. The director Holstein turns him down. Nobody had sent for him and nothing was arranged. He had crossed the Great Belt on the strength of a fourteen-year-old's plan and no other security.
suggested_refs: The Royal Danish Theatre on Kongens Nytorv as it stood in 1819, before the 1874 rebuilding

stops.name: Copenhagen, Siboni's singing school
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month: mid-September 1819 per the H.C. Andersen Centre timetable; day approximate
stops.campa: In the middle of September the Italian Giuseppe Siboni, newly head of the theatre's singing school, hears the boy's soprano at a dinner party, takes him on for lessons and meals, and a subscription is got up among the guests to keep him fed. He is fourteen, cannot spell, and is now inside the building he had tried to storm. One evening a singer takes him by the hand, wishes him happiness on his debut, and leads him to the footlights to present him to the Danish public as a joke.
stops.quote: The people would laugh at me--I felt it; the tears rolled down my cheeks; I tore myself loose, and left the stage full of anguish.
stops.quote_source: The True Story of My Life: A Sketch, Project Gutenberg #7007; verbatim, including the em dash of the source text
suggested_refs: The singing school of the Royal Theatre under Giuseppe Siboni, 1819-1822

stops.name: Copenhagen, the voice breaks
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not established, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: His voice breaks and the singing school has no further use for him. Dancing has already failed. Acting has failed. He turns to writing plays and submitting them to the same theatre that has rejected him in every other capacity, and the theatre rejects those too, with the observation that the author cannot spell. In the same year he prints his first story, The Ghost at Palnatoke's Grave, at his own expense. The board reaches its verdict. The boy is to be sent to school.
suggested_refs: The rejected play manuscripts submitted to the Royal Theatre board, 1822

stops.name: Slagelse, the grammar school under Meisling
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; much English material gives 1823, which the H.C. Andersen Centre 1822 timetable and Danish Wikipedia contradict
stops.campa: Jonas Collin arranges three hundred and fifty rigsdaler a year for three years out of the royal trust fund ad usus publicos, approved by Frederik VI, and on the twenty-sixth of October the seventeen-year-old enters the Latin grammar school at Slagelse among boys of eleven. The rector, Simon Meisling, is a classicist of real learning and a bully. Andersen sits at the bottom of the form. He is forbidden to write verse and writes it anyway, in secret, and shows it to the wrong man.
stops.quote: I could also scarcely spell a word correctly.
stops.quote_source: The True Story of My Life: A Sketch, Project Gutenberg #7007; Andersen on his charity-school education
suggested_refs: The royal trust fund ad usus publicos and its grant to Andersen, 1822-1825

stops.name: Helsingør, the darkest years
stops.date_confidence: attested for the period 1826-1827; month and day of the transfer not established, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Meisling is moved to the school at Helsingør and takes his worst pupil with him, lodging him in his own house. Andersen calls these the darkest and most bitter years of his life and describes the abuse in detail long afterward. The rector reads the poem The Dying Child and gives his verdict. Collin, when he finally learns what is happening, removes the boy in 1827 and has him privately tutored in Copenhagen. Kronborg stands a mile up the shore, Shakespeare's Elsinore, and no account survives of Andersen going inside it.
stops.quote: he read it, and pronounced it to be sentimentality and idle trash.
stops.quote_source: The True Story of My Life: A Sketch, Project Gutenberg #7007; Simon Meisling on Andersen's poem 'The Dying Child'
suggested_refs: The Latin school at Helsingør and the rector's house where Andersen lodged, 1826-1827

stops.name: Copenhagen, the student examination
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not established, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: He passes the entrance examination to the University of Copenhagen and the school ordeal closes. He is twenty-three, holds a certificate, and holds also a permanent conviction that he was educated badly and late. The city he re-enters is small enough that everyone who matters can be met at five dinner tables. Fichte had fled the French occupation of Prussia to this same city while Andersen was an infant in Odense; six years earlier its university had given Gauss the prize for the conformal-mapping memoir, while Andersen was construing Latin at Slagelse.
suggested_refs: The University of Copenhagen matriculation records for 1828

segments.name: Walking Out: Amager, Faaborg, the Harz

stops.name: Copenhagen, a journey on foot to the east point of Amager
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not established, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: He publishes A Journey on Foot from Holmen's Canal to the East Point of Amager, a fantastical walk across his own city in the manner of Hoffmann, and it sells. The vaudeville he writes the same season is staged. At twenty-four he is suddenly an author with a public. The route he invents runs from the canal by the theatre out to the flat edge of Amager, three miles of ground a man can cover on foot in an afternoon: the first of the journeys, and the only one that never leaves Copenhagen.
suggested_refs: Fodreise fra Holmens Canal til Østpynten af Amager (1829), first edition

stops.name: Faaborg, Riborg Voigt
stops.date_confidence: year given by the sources; month and day not established, defaulted to 01-01, and the surrounding tradition is unverifiable in its detail
stops.campa: Visiting a school friend at Faaborg he meets the friend's sister, Riborg Voigt, and falls in love without return. She is already promised. The tradition every Danish biography repeats, and none can substantiate, is that he carried her farewell letter in a leather pouch on a string around his neck for the rest of his life and that it was found there when he died. He never marries. The list of the unreturned will run through Louise Collin and Jenny Lind, and through Edvard Collin, to whom he wrote letters nobody has read as friendship alone.
suggested_refs: The Voigt family house at Faaborg, and the pouch tradition reported by Danish biographers
sources: Wullschlager (2000) and Bredsdorff (1975), cited at second hand

stops.name: The Brocken, the first mountain abroad
stops.date_confidence: attested to the journey, May to June 1831; the Brocken ascent falls in the first half of June, exact day not established
stops.campa: He leaves Copenhagen on the sixteenth of May, partly to get over Riborg Voigt, and is in Hamburg three days later: the first journey out of Denmark. He climbs the Brocken, highest of the Harz and the mountain the Walpurgis legends belong to, and folds it into the travel book he writes that summer. Shadow Pictures of a Journey to the Harz is the discovery of his method. He does not describe places. He describes himself arriving at them, and the arrival is the story, and he will do it for forty years.
suggested_refs: Skyggebilleder fra en Reise til Harzen, det sachsiske Schweitz etc. etc. i Sommeren 1831
sources: Skyggebilleder fra en Reise til Harzen (1831)

stops.name: Dresden and Saxon Switzerland, the way home
stops.date_confidence: attested: Dresden reached 3 June 1831, Copenhagen regained 24 June 1831
stops.campa: From the Harz he goes on into Saxon Switzerland and reaches Dresden on the third of June, and is back in Copenhagen on the twenty-fourth, five weeks after leaving. Thirty more journeys will follow this one. He keeps a diary on every one, sleeps badly in strange rooms, carries a coil of rope against hotel fires, fears being buried alive, and goes anyway, further and more often than any Danish writer of the century. The fear and the going are the same man and never resolve into one another.
suggested_refs: The Elbe sandstone country of Saxon Switzerland as described in the 1831 travel book
sources: Skyggebilleder fra en Reise til Harzen (1831)

stops.name: Paris, Heine and Hugo
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: Paris 10 May to 15 August 1833, Heine met 25 June, Hugo visited 14 August
stops.campa: A royal travelling stipend puts him on the road in April and in Paris by the tenth of May, where he stays until the middle of August. He hears Heinrich Heine lecture and meets him on the twenty-fifth of June, and calls on Victor Hugo on the fourteenth of August. Twelve years on, Karl Marx will be expelled from this same city and count Heine the friend he most hates leaving behind. Andersen's mother dies in Odense on the seventh of October, while he is somewhere on the road south, and the news takes weeks to find him.
suggested_refs: The Paris literary salons of 1833; Andersen's diary of the Heine meeting, 25 June
sources: corpus interlock: karl_marx.journey.json, luc_olivier_merson.journey.json (canonical Paris pin)

stops.name: Le Locle, Agnete and the Merman
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: 25 August to 14 September 1833, with part two of the poem posted home 12 September
stops.campa: From Paris he goes up into the Jura and lodges from the twenty-fifth of August with the Houriets, a Swiss watchmaking family at Le Locle whose Copenhagen connection brought the invitation. Danish accounts often call the family Danish; they were not. In three weeks in the mountains he writes the dramatic poem Agnete and the Merman and posts the second part home on the twelfth of September. It fails in Denmark. The Copenhagen papers have decided that Andersen is a provincial who writes too fast, and will not change their minds for a decade.
suggested_refs: Agnete og Havmanden (1834), written at Le Locle in the Jura

stops.name: Genoa, the coast road south
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed from the 1833 route between Le Locle, left 14 September, and Rome, reached 18 October; exact Genoa dates not established
stops.campa: He crosses the Alps into Lombardy and comes down to the Ligurian coast at Genoa, a working port stacked up a hillside above its harbour. Italy takes hold of him at once and does not let go for the rest of his life: the light, the noise, a poverty that looks nothing like Danish poverty, the singing in the street, the churches open all day. Everything on this coast road goes into the novel he has not yet begun. He is twenty-eight and has never seen a country where the poor are warm.
suggested_refs: The Ligurian coast road of 1833 and its transposition into The Improvisatore

stops.name: Sestri Levante, the bay
stops.date_confidence: the evening is attested to 1833; the exact date is not established and is placed on the reconstructed coast route
stops.campa: He spends an evening in the fishing village of Sestri Levante, on a bay between two headlands. Nothing recorded happens there. More than a century later the town names the bay the Baia delle Favole, the Bay of Fables, after him, and hangs an international prize for fairy tales on the name. The honour is entirely posthumous and rests on a single night's lodging. The town has no other claim on him. What it keeps is what a man who wrote fables leaves behind in a place he passed through once.
suggested_refs: The Baia delle Favole at Sestri Levante, named for Andersen in the twentieth century, and its fairy-tale prize
sources: Wikipedia, 'Hans Christian Andersen' (the naming is a later civic honour, not a contemporary event)

stops.name: Rome, the Caffè Greco and Thorvaldsen
stops.date_confidence: contested and resolved: English Wikipedia gives October 1834, the H.C. Andersen Centre gives 18 October 1833 with a chronology that hangs together; the Centre is followed and the disagreement is left visible
stops.campa: He reaches Rome on the eighteenth of October and stays until February, taking his coffee at the Caffè Greco below the Spanish Steps among the colony of Scandinavian artists. Bertel Thorvaldsen, the most famous Dane alive, is working in the city and takes to him. On the twenty-seventh of December he begins The Improvisatore. His mother has been dead eleven days when he arrives and he does not yet know it. English Wikipedia dates this arrival to October 1834, a full year late, and the error has travelled far.
suggested_refs: The Caffè Greco on Via dei Condotti, meeting place of the Scandinavian colony in Rome
sources: Wikipedia, 'Hans Christian Andersen' (contradicted on the year)

stops.name: Vesuvius and Pompeii, the buried city
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1834 during the Naples leg, which follows the departure from Rome on 12 February; month approximate, day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: South to Naples, where he climbs Vesuvius while it is in eruption and walks the excavated streets of Pompeii. Both go straight into The Improvisatore, the eruption as set piece, the dead city as the book's memory of what buries people and keeps them. He is twenty-nine, unattached, two thousand miles from Odense, living on a grant from the kingdom that raised him out of a washerwoman's room. He turns north in the spring and recrosses the Alps by way of Florence, carrying a novel he has not finished.
suggested_refs: The Vesuvius eruption sequence and the Pompeii pages of The Improvisatore (1835)

stops.name: Copenhagen, The Improvisatore
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not established from reachable sources, defaulted within the spring of 1835
stops.campa: The Improvisatore appears in Copenhagen, an Italian novel by a Dane who had been in Italy less than a year, and it is the first of his books to be taken seriously abroad. Germany translates it inside the year. The Danish reviewers grant him talent and add, as they always add, that he is uneducated. He is already writing something else, in a form nobody asked him for, which he does not think of as his principal work, and which his publisher will print as a sixty-one page pamphlet at a low price.
suggested_refs: Improvisatoren (1835), first edition, C. A. Reitzel, Copenhagen

stops.name: Copenhagen, the first booklet of tales
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the eighth of May C. A. Reitzel publishes sixty-one pages titled Eventyr, fortalte for Børn: The Tinderbox, Little Claus and Big Claus, The Princess and the Pea, Little Ida's Flowers. The reviews are bad. He is told the tone is too colloquial for print, that a serious author does not write down to anyone, that the form has no future in Danish letters. A second booklet with Thumbelina and The Traveling Companion follows on the sixteenth of December. He goes on issuing them, a few tales at a time, for thirty-seven years.
suggested_refs: Eventyr, fortalte for Børn, first booklet, C. A. Reitzel, Copenhagen, 8 May 1835
sources: Bredsdorff (1975) and the H.C. Andersen Centre bibliography, cited at second hand

stops.name: Copenhagen, the third booklet: the Little Mermaid
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: The third booklet, seventh of April 1837, carries The Little Mermaid and The Emperor's New Clothes. One is about a creature who gives up her voice and her element for a man who marries somebody else, and who dissolves rather than kill him. The other is about a crowd agreeing to see what is not there until a child says otherwise. Both are printed for children. Neither ends the way a story for children ends, and it is these two, not the novels, that carry his name out of Danish and keep it out.
suggested_refs: Eventyr, fortalte for Børn, third booklet, 7 April 1837
sources: Wikipedia, 'List of works by Hans Christian Andersen'

stops.name: Nysø Manor, the permanent guest
stops.date_confidence: the visits run from 1839 across the 1850s; no single date attaches, so the opening year is used with month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Baroness Christine Stampe and Baron Henrik Stampe keep Nysø near Præstø, and build a studio in the garden for Thorvaldsen, who works there through his last years. Andersen is a house guest across more than a decade, writing in the mornings and reading aloud after dinner to whoever is at the table. He has no household of his own and will never have one. The manors of Zealand and Funen, Nysø and Glorup and Holsteinborg, are where he lives between journeys, a permanent guest with a trunk and a rope.
suggested_refs: Thorvaldsen's garden studio at Nysø, built for him by the Stampes
sources: biographies of Christine Stampe and Thorvaldsen, cited at second hand

stops.name: Trieste, taking ship on the Adriatic
stops.date_confidence: the journey begins in autumn 1840 and reaches Greece in spring 1841; the Trieste leg is placed at December, month approximate
stops.campa: He goes down through Germany and Italy to Trieste and takes ship on the Adriatic, bound for Greece and the Ottoman capital: the longest journey of his life and the one he will make his best travel book of. He is thirty-five. The Danish press is still condescending and the German press is not, and he has begun to notice a rule that will hold for the rest of his life, that his reputation improves in exact proportion to the distance from Copenhagen.
suggested_refs: En Digters Bazar (1842), the record of the 1840-41 journey to Greece and Constantinople

stops.name: Athens, the Acropolis
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: He lands in Greece and is in Athens on the twenty-fourth of March, a capital nine years old, the Parthenon standing above a town of a few thousand under a Bavarian king. He climbs the Acropolis. What he writes about it in A Poet's Bazaar is not archaeology and does not pretend to be; it is a Dane in his thirties on a hill of broken marble, setting down what the place does to a man who grew up in two rooms by a river in Odense and has now walked up to the thing itself.
suggested_refs: The Acropolis of Athens in 1841, before the great clearances of the later nineteenth century

stops.name: Constantinople, Hagia Sophia
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1841 during the Ottoman leg; exact day of the Hagia Sophia visit not established, month approximate
stops.campa: From Greece he crosses to Constantinople and enters Hagia Sophia, a mosque these four centuries, and gives the building more pages than he gave the Acropolis. He is in the city for the Sultan's birthday procession and describes the crowds at length. He had meant to go home overland through the Balkans and is warned off by news of insurrection in Rumelia, so he takes the river instead, which is how the last third of the book comes to be a steamboat log.
suggested_refs: Hagia Sophia as a mosque in 1841, and the Sultan's birthday procession described in A Poet's Bazaar

stops.name: The Iron Gates, up the Danube
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1841 return leg; exact day of the gorge passage not established, month approximate
stops.campa: The Danube steamer carries him up through the Iron Gates, the gorge where the river narrows between the Carpathian and Balkan walls and the boats of that decade have to be hauled through against the current. He renders the passage in detail: quarantine stops, cholera rumours, the rock closing in on both sides, the noise of the water. The route home is the modern one, steam and timetable and printed fare, out of the oldest country he has ever stood in.
suggested_refs: The Iron Gates gorge before the twentieth-century damming, as described in A Poet's Bazaar

stops.name: Vienna, the Stephansdom and the way back
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1841 return leg; month approximate, day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The Danube sets him down at Vienna, and the spire of the Stephansdom is the sign that he is back inside the Europe he knows. A Poet's Bazaar comes out the following year, issued in parts. He has now gone from the Baltic to the Bosphorus and written all of it down, in a decade when most Danish writers of his standing have seen Germany and stopped there. The journey costs him the better part of a year and earns him, at home in Copenhagen, the observation that he travels too much and writes it up too fast.
suggested_refs: En Digters Bazar (1842), published in parts, with dedications including Liszt and Thorvaldsen

segments.name: The Celebrity: Weimar, Berlin, Nyhavn, England

stops.name: Weimar, the Grand Duke
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1844; the Weimar stay precedes the Berlin visit of 23-31 July, exact dates not established, day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He comes to Weimar, where Goethe ran the court theatre and turned a duchy of a few thousand souls into the literary capital of the German language, and finds the grandson of Goethe's duke on the point of inheriting it. Carl Alexander is twenty-six. The friendship holds in letters for the rest of Andersen's life, and the Grand Duke will make him a Knight of the White Falcon. Goethe has been dead twelve years. Andersen walks the same short streets and is received in the house on the Frauenplan.
suggested_refs: The Andersen correspondence with Carl Alexander of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach

stops.name: Berlin, Unter den Linden: Grimm has not heard of him
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the pool and much secondary material place this meeting in 1845-46, which the H.C. Andersen Centre 1844 timetable contradicts
stops.campa: In Berlin on the twenty-sixth of July he calls on Jacob Grimm, the greatest living collector of folk tales, and Grimm has never heard of him. The two men stand in a doorway, one of them explaining who he is. The order is usually told the other way round, with Andersen arriving preceded by his German fame; the German fame arrives a year or two later, in the celebrated Berlin seasons of 1845 and 1846. In the summer of 1844 the man who collected the tales does not know the man who wrote them.
suggested_refs: The H.C. Andersen Centre 1844 timetable entry for the Grimm call, 26 July
sources: Wikipedia, 'Hans Christian Andersen' (contradicted on the date and the framing)

stops.name: Copenhagen, Nyhavn 67
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the move; month and day not established, defaulted to 01-01; he keeps the rooms until 1864
stops.campa: He takes rooms at Nyhavn 67, on the canal where the coasters unload, and keeps them for nearly twenty years. It is the closest thing to a home he ever has, and it is rented, on a waterfront of sailors and cheap lodgings. Copenhagen holds a hundred and thirty thousand people and every one of them knows him by sight: very tall, very thin, walking fast. Niels Bohr is born forty years later a short walk along the same water at Ved Stranden, and the institute Bohr raises at Blegdamsvej brings Heisenberg and Dirac through these streets in their turn.
suggested_refs: The memorial plaque at Nyhavn 67, Copenhagen

stops.name: London, Gore House: meeting Dickens
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1847; exact day of the Gore House party not established, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The Countess of Blessington gives a party at Gore House in Kensington and Andersen meets Charles Dickens there for the first time. Mary Howitt's translations have gone ahead of him and England receives him as a celebrity. He calls it a triumphant season and means it. Dickens sends him a set of his own works, inscribed, and sees him off at Ramsgate. Andersen goes home believing he has made the friend of his life, and for ten years there is nothing in the correspondence to tell him otherwise.
suggested_refs: Mary Howitt, Wonderful Stories for Children (1846), the first English Andersen
sources: Zipes, The Misunderstood Storyteller (2005), cited at second hand

stops.name: Trollhättan, the falls and the telegraph
stops.date_confidence: the Swedish travels are dated 1849 and the book follows in 1851; month and day not established, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: He travels in Sweden and stands at the falls of Trollhättan, where the locks step the boats down past the white water. In the book that follows he sets the falls against the telegraph wire and the railway and comes down, without hesitation, in favour of both. The poet of tinderboxes and mermaids is an enthusiast for machinery. In Sweden ends in an essay in praise of the new century's inventions, written by a man who was born before the steamship reached Denmark.
suggested_refs: I Sverrig (In Sweden, 1851) and its closing essay on the new inventions

stops.name: Gads Hill Place, five weeks instead of two
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1857; the visit runs some five weeks in the summer, exact arrival day not established, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Dickens invites him to Gads Hill Place in Kent for a fortnight and he stays five weeks. He speaks little English. The household that had been warm to him in London ten years earlier is worn through by the time he leaves, and after he goes Dickens simply stops answering his letters. Andersen does not understand what has happened and keeps writing for years. The friendship does not end in a quarrel or by agreement between two men. One of them falls silent and the other does not notice for a long time.
suggested_refs: Gads Hill Place, Higham, Kent, the Dickens house from 1856

stops.name: Copenhagen, Harald Scharff
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the Collin reproach; the pool and some secondary sources give 1861 for the whole episode, which the H.C. Andersen Centre 1862 timetable contradicts
stops.campa: He is fifty-six and the dancer Harald Scharff is twenty-six, and through the winter the two are inseparable. Theodor Collin reproaches him about it on the seventeenth of February; on the fifth of March he speaks to Einar Drewsen of his erotic time. It is the only period of his life he describes in those words, and the biographers who call it his erotic period are quoting him. It ends on the thirteenth of November of the following year. What it was, the diaries do not settle, and no later account has settled it either.
suggested_refs: Andersen's diaries and almanacs for February and March 1862
sources: Wikipedia, 'Hans Christian Andersen' (interpretive framing by biographers)

stops.name: Granada, the Alhambra
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1862 Spanish journey; the Granada leg falls in the autumn, exact date not established, day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He goes to Spain, a country few Danish writers had bothered with, and reaches the Alhambra at Granada. By 1862 the Moorish palace is the obligatory stop of European romanticism, Irving's Tales thirty years in print and the courts full of visitors doing exactly what Andersen is doing. He does it anyway and writes In Spain. He also sees Madrid and Toledo. He is fifty-seven and still moves like a man who believes there is a country left that he has not seen.
suggested_refs: I Spanien (In Spain, 1863)

stops.name: Setúbal, the Quinta dos Bonecos
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: Setúbal 8 June to 9 July 1866; the sources frequently name the wrong O'Neill brother for this stay
stops.campa: From the eighth of June to the ninth of July he stays at the Quinta dos Bonecos near Setúbal with Carlos O'Neill, of an Irish family long settled in Portugal, whom Andersen had known some forty years, since his student days in Copenhagen. George O'Neill, the Danish consul-general, has him in Lisbon before and after; José O'Neill takes him to Cintra. A Visit to Portugal in 1866 is published two years later, in 1868. It is his last travel book and the last of the long journeys.
suggested_refs: Et Besøg i Portugal 1866, published 1868, Andersen's last travel book
sources: Wikipedia, 'Hans Christian Andersen' (contradicted on the host and the publication year)

stops.name: Paris, the Champ de Mars
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1867; exact dates of the Exposition visit not established, defaulted within the run of the fair
stops.campa: He goes to the Exposition Universelle on the Champ de Mars, the fair of the Second Empire at its height, and walks the machine hall among the crowds. He is sixty-two and internationally famous, in a Paris he first entered thirty-four years earlier on a student's stipend to hear Heine lecture. Luc-Olivier Merson is twenty-one that year and at the Beaux-Arts across the river. This is one of the last of the thirty journeys. He has eight years to live.
suggested_refs: The Exposition Universelle of 1867 on the Champ de Mars
sources: H.C. Andersen Centre, later travel chronology

stops.name: Odense Rådhus, honorary citizen
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: On the sixth of December Odense makes him an honorary citizen, with a torchlit procession through the streets he had walked as the washerwoman's son. The town that gave him a charity school and two rooms by the river now spells his name in light on its own town hall, and he stands at the window while it does. Forty-eight years earlier he left in the Nyborg mail coach with thirteen rigsdaler, having been advised, by the highest authority the town could produce, to learn a respectable trade.
suggested_refs: The Odense honorary-citizenship ceremony and torchlit procession, 6 December 1867

stops.name: Rolighed, the Melchiors' house
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the villa is demolished and the coordinate is a reconstruction of the site, not a survey
stops.campa: He dies on the morning of the fourth of August at Rolighed, the country house of the banker Moritz Melchior and his wife, who had taken him in through the last illness. He is seventy. The liver cancer declared itself in the year or two before; the fall from his bed in 1872 had ended his strength earlier than that, and the last new tales had appeared the same year. He had given an instruction about the funeral music. The villa is gone now and the pin is a reconstruction of where it stood.
stops.quote: Most of the people who will walk after me will be children, so make the beat keep time with little steps.
stops.quote_source: Andersen's reported deathbed instruction about his funeral music, quoted on English Wikipedia at footnote 50; not traced to a primary source, tagged R
suggested_refs: The site of Rolighed, the Melchior villa north of Copenhagen, since demolished

stops.name: Assistens Kirkegård, section P
stops.date_confidence: the burial follows the death of 4 August 1875; the exact day is not established from reachable sources and is placed within the week after
stops.campa: He is buried in section P of Assistens Kirkegård at Nørrebro, in the Collin family plot, under a stone that originally carried three names: his own, Edvard Collin's, and Henriette Collin's. Edvard is the man he loved longest and least successfully, who withheld the familiar du from him for decades and got letters about it that scholars still argue over. The arrangement of the grave has been read as a last statement of that attachment. It is also simply where his patrons were buried, and he was their household's dependent for fifty years.
suggested_refs: The Collin family plot, section P no. 513, Assistens Kirkegård, Nørrebro
sources: Danish Wikipedia, 'Assistens Kirkegård, København' (coordinate and plot)

stops.name: Langelinie, the bronze on the rock
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: A bronze girl by Edvard Eriksen is set on a rock at the Langelinie promenade, commissioned by the brewer Carl Jacobsen after a ballet on the tale moved him. She is not quite a mermaid and not quite a woman, which is the story. Her head is sawn off in 1964 and never found, and a new one cast from the mould; an arm goes in 1984 and comes back in two days; the head goes again in 1998 and is returned anonymously; explosives take her off the rock in 2003. In 1970 the medal that carries Andersen's name goes to Maurice Sendak at Bologna, the first American to take it.
suggested_refs: Edvard Eriksen's Den lille Havfrue, Langelinie, unveiled 23 August 1913, and its vandalism record
sources: Carlsberg Foundation and Copenhagen city historical accounts
